metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready swimming knowledge for non-swimmers, fearful beginners, and early fitness swimmers. The draft emphasizes water competency, supervision, safe pool behavior, breathing, floating, gliding, progressive learn-to-swim gates, anxiety-aware teaching, drowning-prevention safeguards, and fitness-app constraints that prevent unsafe prescriptions for users who cannot yet swim safely.

source_refs.title: Preventing Drowning
source_refs.organization_or_author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_refs.notes: Used for layered prevention: swim lessons, close supervision, four-sided pool fencing, life jackets, CPR, natural-water risks, buddy system, alcohol avoidance, and the principle that drowning can happen quickly and quietly.

source_refs.title: Risk Factors for Drowning
source_refs.organization_or_author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_refs.notes: Used for risk stratification around children, weak swimmers, inability to swim, males, seizure disorders, heart conditions, autism spectrum disorder, life jackets, and pool fencing.

source_refs.title: Water Safety
source_refs.notes: Used for core water competency skills: enter deep water and surface, float or tread, turn, swim 25 yards, exit, adapt to water environment, use water watchers, and use reach-or-throw rescue principles.

source_refs.title: Water Competency
source_refs.notes: Used for the distinction between novice water competency and good swimming, arm's-reach supervision for children without basic skills, water watchers, and safe simple rescue from the water's edge.

source_refs.title: AAP Releases Updated Drowning Prevention Recommendations
source_refs.notes: Used for 2026 recommendations on touch supervision, swim lessons after the first birthday when developmentally ready, life jackets for young children and non-swimmers, CPR, and the warning that swim lessons are only one prevention layer.

source_refs.title: Swim Lessons for Children: When to Start and What to Consider
source_refs.notes: Used for readiness factors, parent-child lessons, survival skills, the no-drown-proofing message, and quality markers for instruction such as qualified teachers and lifeguards.

source_refs.title: WHO Guideline on the Prevention of Drowning: Basic Swim Skills and Water Safety Training
source_refs.notes: Used for the recommendation that basic swim skills and water safety training programs be provided to children aged 6 years or older, and for implementation cautions about safe environments, acceptable instructional techniques, and possible risk tolerance after training.

source_refs.title: Learn-to-Swim
source_refs.notes: Used for the life-skill framing of swimming, formal lesson access, provider quality markers, no child ever being water safe, and the goal of making children safer around water.

source_refs.title: Learn to Swim
source_refs.notes: Used for the principle that water confidence is not the same as competence, the value of completing staged learn-to-swim awards, school swimming targets, self-rescue, inclusion, and adult learner pathways.

source_refs.title: Learn to Swim Stage 1 Award
source_refs.notes: Used for early outcomes: safe entry and exit, movement in multiple directions, water on face, front and back float recovery, front and back push-and-glide, and pool rules.

source_refs.title: Learn to Swim Stage 2 Award
source_refs.notes: Used for progression to safe jump entry, rhythmic bubbles, unsupported floating recovery, front and back glide, basic leg action travel, log rolls, and unsupported exit.

source_refs.title: Learn to Swim Stage 3 Award
source_refs.notes: Used for progression to submersion, streamlined push-offs, log-roll transitions, front/back travel, tuck float, safe exit without steps, and identifying water safety messages.

source_refs.title: Swim England Adult Swimming Framework
source_refs.notes: Used for adult-specific needs: confidence, technique, safety, no age limit, different motivations, and progressive goals for complete beginners through coached improvement.

source_refs.title: Water Safety for Kids
source_refs.notes: Used for Safety Around Water concepts, adjustment to water, Jump Push Turn Grab, Swim Float Swim, supervision messaging, and confidence-building lessons.

source_refs.title: Float to Live
source_refs.notes: Used for floating under stress: head back, breathing control, gentle limb movement, individual buoyancy differences, supervised practice, then calling for help or swimming to safety.

source_refs.title: The Water Safety Code
source_refs.notes: Used for Stop and Think, Stay Together, Call emergency services, Float, lifeguarded venues, open-water cold shock, never entering the water for untrained rescue, and throwing something buoyant.

source_refs.title: Swim to Survive
source_refs.notes: Used for the minimum survival sequence after unexpected deep-water entry: orient at surface, tread for one minute, and swim 50 meters to safety. Also used for the distinction between survival screening and full swimming lessons.

source_refs.title: Swim and Survive
source_refs.notes: Used for progressive swimming, personal survival, basic rescue, lifesaving skills, inclusion across abilities, national benchmarks, and increasing endurance and complexity over time.

source_refs.title: Joint Statement on Hypoxic Blackout and Inaccurate Use of the Terminology Shallow Water Blackout
source_refs.organization_or_author: American Red Cross, YMCA of the USA, and USA Swimming
source_refs.notes: Used for the explicit safety rule against hyperventilation and extended breath-holding, single-inhalation limits before submersion tasks, safety limits for breath-hold activities, and response to motionless swimmers.

source_refs.title: From Swimming Skill to Water Competence: Towards a More Inclusive Drowning Prevention Future
source_refs.notes: Used for the model that drowning prevention requires physical aquatic competencies plus cognitive and affective competencies, not stroke ability alone.

source_refs.title: Association Between Swimming Lessons and Drowning in Childhood: A Case-Control Study
source_refs.notes: Used for evidence that formal swimming lessons were associated with reduced drowning risk in children ages 1-4, while emphasizing imprecision, residual risk, and that swim skills alone are insufficient.

source_refs.title: Systematic Review on Basic Swimming and Water Safety Skills Training for Drowning Prevention
source_refs.organization_or_author: Centre for Evidence-Based Practice, Belgian Red Cross
source_refs.notes: Used for updated synthesis: swim training may reduce mortality and improve skills, water safety training may improve safe behavior, combined programs likely reduce drowning mortality, and shallow-water training is preferred for preschoolers.

source_refs.title: Development and Validity of the Fear of Water Assessment Questionnaire
source_refs.notes: Used for fear of water as a strong predictor of no or low swimming competence, and for the need to identify fear so instruction can use appropriate teaching strategies.

key_concepts.concept: Water competency is broader than lap swimming.
key_concepts.details: A beginner can move through water yet still lack safety skills such as orienting after submersion, floating or treading, turning toward an exit, exiting safely, judging hazards, and avoiding unsafe rescue attempts.

key_concepts.concept: Water confidence and water competence must be tracked separately.
key_concepts.details: A learner may feel relaxed in shallow water but be unable to recover from floating, breathe rhythmically, or exit from deep water. Conversely, a fearful learner may have enough physical ability but need graded exposure before normal skill progression.

key_concepts.concept: Swim lessons are one layer, not a stand-alone safety guarantee.
key_concepts.details: Backend recommendations should combine skill training with supervision, barriers, life jackets where appropriate, CPR readiness, safe venues, and risk-context decisions. Never imply a user is drown-proof.

key_concepts.concept: A non-swimmer should not receive fitness swim workouts.
key_concepts.details: If the user cannot safely enter, surface, float or tread, turn, move to an exit, and exit, the app should prescribe only safety education and in-person learn-to-swim tasks, not yardage, intervals, pace targets, or calorie goals.

key_concepts.concept: Standing-depth competence should precede deep-water tasks.
key_concepts.details: Early practice should allow the learner to stand, use the wall, and recover quickly. Deep-water entry, survival sequences, and unsupported exits require prior proof of breathing, floating, rolling, and recovery.

key_concepts.concept: Relaxed exhalation and breath timing are safety skills before they are stroke skills.
key_concepts.details: Beginners often hold breath, lift the head, rush, or panic. Early lessons should teach calm inhalation above water, steady exhalation into water, recovery to breathing positions, and pausing at the wall.

key_concepts.concept: Floating is a reset and survival behavior, not merely a drill.
key_concepts.details: Back floating allows a struggling swimmer to rest, regain breathing control, call for help, or choose a safer route to exit. Learners need to practice finding their own float because body composition and limb position affect buoyancy.

key_concepts.concept: Rolling connects face immersion, breathing access, and safe travel.
key_concepts.details: The front-to-back and back-to-front roll lets the learner transition from prone travel to breathing, recover from unexpected rotation, and avoid panic when the face submerges.

key_concepts.concept: Supervision means a responsible adult is watching without distraction.
key_concepts.details: For infants, toddlers, weak swimmers, and non-swimmers, the supervising adult should be close enough to intervene immediately. Lifeguards reduce risk but do not replace caregiver or program supervision.

key_concepts.concept: Self-rated swim ability is not enough for safety gating.
key_concepts.details: The app should ask for observable tasks or instructor verification rather than relying on labels like beginner, can swim, or comfortable. Confidence, distance, and survival ability should be assessed separately.

key_concepts.concept: Fear of water is a primary programming variable.
key_concepts.details: Fear may block relaxation, floating, face immersion, breath rhythm, deep-water entry, and lesson attendance. The app should normalize slower progress, avoid forceful prompts, and recommend qualified in-person instruction when fear is high.

key_concepts.concept: Pool rules and safe behavior are part of learn-to-swim competence.
key_concepts.details: Safe entry and exit, walking on deck, obeying lifeguards and posted signs, no rough play, lane awareness, no diving where prohibited, and asking permission before entering water should be stored as teachable outcomes.

key_concepts.concept: Pool competence does not automatically unlock open-water swimming.
key_concepts.details: Currents, waves, cold water, visibility, depth, uneven footing, boats, and distance from exit change the risk profile. Open-water training needs separate readiness and environment checks.

key_concepts.concept: Beginners should learn safe help-seeking and land-based assist principles.
key_concepts.details: The app should teach call for help, alert a lifeguard, phone emergency services, reach or throw a floating object, and avoid untrained in-water rescue because rescuers can become victims.

key_concepts.concept: Water safety skills must be practiced, not treated as one-time achievements.
key_concepts.details: Backend progression should support periodic reassessment after breaks, seasonal gaps, growth changes, injury, fear return, or environment changes.

technical_models.model: Enter or recover to surface, control breathing, float or tread, turn and orient, travel to a safe exit, and exit independently.
technical_models.use_case: Minimum gate before fitness swim prescriptions, deep-water exposure, or unsupervised lap recommendations.

technical_models.model: Acclimate to water, enter and exit safely, move in standing depth, tolerate water on face, exhale bubbles, float front and back, recover to stand, push and glide, roll, kick travel, then link short swim-float-swim sequences.
technical_models.use_case: Default beginner progression for non-swimmers and low-confidence users.

technical_models.model: Breathe in above water, exhale gently into water, pause or roll to breathe when needed, and avoid repeated or extended underwater breath-hold challenges.
technical_models.use_case: Beginner breathing instruction and app safety copy for drills.

technical_models.model: Tilt head back, clear airway, relax the body, allow legs to sink if needed, use gentle sculling or kicking only as required, regain breath, then call for help or move to safety.
technical_models.use_case: Survival reset and anxiety-management skill for beginners.

technical_models.model: Face in water with bubbles, arms and body relaxed, bring knees under body, press or sweep hands as needed, and return to standing or roll to the back.
technical_models.use_case: Safe transition out of prone float and the foundation for freestyle progression.

technical_models.model: Push gently from wall into a long horizontal shape, maintain relaxed head and body alignment, glide briefly, then recover to stand or roll before distress.
technical_models.use_case: Bridge from static float to efficient travel.

technical_models.model: Use a log roll or tuck rotation to move between front and back positions so the swimmer can access air, reorient, and continue safely.
technical_models.use_case: Water confidence, survival sequence, and freestyle readiness.

technical_models.model: After an unexpected or deliberate entry, regain surface control, push away only if needed, turn toward the wall or exit, and grab support.
technical_models.use_case: Survival skill for children and new swimmers in pool settings.

technical_models.model: Travel briefly, roll or transition to float for breathing and rest, then resume travel toward the exit.
technical_models.use_case: Early endurance without panic or forced continuous swimming.

technical_models.model: Unexpected deep-water entry is handled as orient, support at surface for one minute, and swim to safety for 50 meters.
technical_models.use_case: Survival benchmark after pool-based basics are established; not a replacement for full stroke instruction.

technical_models.model: Progress from dry orientation and poolside observation to seated entry, standing-depth movement, face wetting, breath bubbles, supported float, independent float, roll, shallow travel, then deep-water practice with qualified supervision.
technical_models.use_case: Fearful adults, trauma history, or learners who panic with face immersion or depth.

technical_models.model: Assign one responsible watcher who is undistracted, not impaired, able to intervene or summon help, and close enough for the swimmer's ability level.
technical_models.use_case: Safety prerequisite for children, non-swimmers, weak swimmers, and fearful beginners.

technical_models.model: Recognize distress, shout or signal for help, call emergency services, alert lifeguard, reach or throw flotation from land, and avoid entering water unless trained and necessary.
technical_models.use_case: Beginner water safety education and app emergency guidance.

technical_models.model: Adults may require privacy, autonomy, explanation, slower exposure, and goals linked to family safety, recreation, fitness, or confidence rather than child-style awards.
technical_models.use_case: Adult non-swimmer onboarding and adherence support.

tactical_rules.rule: If basic water competency is missing, do not prescribe laps, intervals, distance targets, pace targets, timed tests, or calorie-focused swim workouts.
tactical_rules.rationale: Fitness stress can amplify panic and fatigue before the user has safe recovery options.

tactical_rules.rule: Non-swimmers, weak swimmers, children, and fearful beginners require qualified in-person supervision; children or weak swimmers should be kept within immediate reach where applicable.
tactical_rules.rationale: Beginner skills do not remove the need for active supervision, and drowning can be fast and quiet.

tactical_rules.rule: Never prescribe hyperventilation, maximum underwater distance, repeated breath-hold challenges, or extended underwater kicking to beginners.
tactical_rules.rationale: Extended breath-holding and hyperventilation can cause hypoxic blackout and drowning.

tactical_rules.rule: Initial water-confidence, bubble, float, and glide tasks should occur in shallow water where the learner can stand and recover, unless a qualified instructor decides otherwise.
tactical_rules.rationale: Standing-depth practice reduces panic cost and allows immediate recovery while skill is incomplete.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginner drills should keep the wall, steps, lane rope, instructor, or safe support close enough for immediate recovery.
tactical_rules.rationale: The learner needs a predictable exit from uncertainty while breathing, floating, and orientation skills are still fragile.

tactical_rules.rule: Deep-water tasks should remain locked until the learner can float or tread, turn, travel to safety, and exit under supervision.
tactical_rules.rationale: Deep water removes the option to stand and exposes gaps in float, breath, and orientation skills.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not provide diving, start, or head-first entry instructions to non-swimmers or beginners unless pool rules allow it, depth is safe, and a qualified instructor is present.
tactical_rules.rationale: Head-first entry adds collision, depth, and spinal injury risk outside the learn-to-swim foundation.

tactical_rules.rule: Recommend lifeguarded pools or supervised lesson venues for beginner practice.
tactical_rules.rationale: A controlled facility with trained responders is more appropriate than informal water access for early learners.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not treat inflatable toys, water wings, noodles, or foam play aids as safety devices.
tactical_rules.rationale: They can deflate, slip, or create false confidence; approved life jackets are the relevant safety device where needed.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginner rescue education should prioritize call, alert, reach, throw, and encourage floating; do not prompt untrained users to enter water for rescue.
tactical_rules.rationale: An untrained rescuer can become a second victim.

tactical_rules.rule: If the learner panics, repeatedly inhales water, cannot regain breathing, becomes exhausted, or refuses the next step, stop the task and return to supported shallow work.
tactical_rules.rationale: Pushing through panic can reinforce fear and increase immediate safety risk.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not unlock open-water workouts from pool-based beginner success alone.
tactical_rules.rationale: Cold water, currents, waves, visibility, depth, and distance from exit create different hazards.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not recommend swimming practice when the user reports alcohol use, sedating medication effects, impaired judgment, or poor balance.
tactical_rules.rationale: Impairment degrades coordination, judgment, and supervision quality.

tactical_rules.rule: Users with seizure disorder, cardiac history, autism-related wandering risk, severe fear, disability requiring adaptation, or prior near-drowning should be directed to qualified in-person instruction and medical or caregiver guidance where appropriate.
tactical_rules.rationale: Some users need individualized safety planning beyond app-led progressions.

physical_demands.demand: Beginners must coordinate breathing while the face is wet, the mouth and nose are intermittently submerged, and anxiety may increase respiratory rate.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Use short exposures, bubbles, wall recovery, and floating resets before any continuous swimming demand.

physical_demands.demand: Floating requires relaxation, airway control, body position awareness, and acceptance that legs may sink differently across users.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Avoid rigid one-size-fits-all float cues; teach individual float discovery and recovery to stand or roll.

physical_demands.demand: Unexpected water entry or face immersion requires the swimmer to locate the surface, wall, exit, or instructor while managing breathing.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Train turning, rolling, grabbing the wall, and safe exit before endurance.

physical_demands.demand: Rolling, submerging, and changing body position in water can challenge balance and orientation.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Progress from supported rotations to independent log rolls and tucks only when the learner remains calm.

physical_demands.demand: Swimming lacks ground impact but water safety risk is high for beginners because fatigue, panic, and breath disruption can escalate quickly.
physical_demands.training_relevance: The app should treat beginner swimming as a safety and skill domain, not simply cardio with lower joint load.

physical_demands.demand: New swimmers fatigue quickly in the neck, trunk, hips, shoulders, and breathing muscles because inefficient body position creates drag.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Use short repeats with generous rest and wall contact; stop before technique or breathing collapses.

physical_demands.demand: Water on the face, ears submerged, bubbles, sound changes, and eye irritation can be major barriers for anxious beginners.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Water acclimation tasks should be explicit and optional enough to avoid overwhelming the learner.

physical_demands.demand: Beginners need enough leg, arm, and trunk control to use steps, ladders, wall exits, or shallow-water standing recovery.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Assess entry and exit ability before swim tasks, especially for children, older adults, larger bodies, and users with mobility limitations.

physical_demands.demand: Cold water, waves, currents, unclear water, and distance from support increase breathing and decision stress.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Open-water plans require a separate safety model with lifeguarded venues, visibility, conditions, buddy system, and flotation decisions.

physical_demands.demand: A beginner must interpret rules, hazards, body sensations, breath cues, instructor prompts, and fear signals at the same time.
physical_demands.training_relevance: Give one task at a time, use predictable session structure, and avoid performance pressure.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Non-swimmers and weak swimmers can drown during seemingly simple practice if supervision, wall access, or recovery skills are absent.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Require active supervision, shallow water, wall access, and explicit stop conditions for all early tasks.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Hyperventilation, prolonged underwater swimming, and breath-holding challenges can lead to loss of consciousness in water.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Block all breath-hold prescriptions and teach exhalation, single-breath submersion limits, and immediate surfacing when the urge to breathe occurs.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Fear, unexpected submersion, deep water, or inability to stand can trigger panic, which disrupts breathing and decision making.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Use graded exposure, shallow water, learner choice, instructor support, and floating resets.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeatedly inhaling or swallowing water may indicate breath-control failure, distress, or task mismatch.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Stop the set, return to bubbles and supported float recovery, and do not resume until breathing is calm.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Caregivers or users may reduce supervision because a learner has completed lessons or can swim a short distance.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: App copy must state that lessons make users safer, not safe; maintain layers of protection and regular reassessment.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Deep water removes the option to stand, so a minor breathing or floating failure can become a major safety problem.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Keep deep-water tasks locked until observed or verified float/tread, turn, travel, and exit skills are present.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Cold shock, currents, waves, poor visibility, underwater hazards, and distance from exit can overwhelm pool-trained beginners.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Require open-water-specific safety education, lifeguarded locations, buddy system, conditions check, and no beginner solo swims.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Pool decks, ladders, steps, and uncontrolled jumps can cause falls, collisions, or head and spine injury.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Teach walk-on-deck, safe entry, safe exit, no diving unless cleared, and obey all facility rules.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: If a beginner progresses directly to lap volume with poor technique, shoulder, neck, and back irritation can develop alongside safety fatigue.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Unlock short technique bouts before continuous swims, monitor symptoms, and avoid paddles or high-resistance tools.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Seizure disorders, cardiac conditions, autism-related wandering risk, medications affecting balance or judgment, and impairment can increase drowning risk.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Collect risk flags, recommend medical or caregiver planning, require supervision, and avoid solo swimming recommendations.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Overuse of flotation aids, goggles, snorkels, or noodles may hide gaps in breath control, floating, and unsupported recovery.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Use aids only as temporary teaching supports and separately assess unsupported safety skills.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Phones, conversation, alcohol, or assuming someone else is watching can create supervision gaps.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Prompt explicit water-watcher assignment and distraction-free supervision in child and weak-swimmer contexts.

training_implications.implication: Swimming onboarding should ask about water confidence, ability to float or tread, breath control, continuous distance, deep-water comfort, exit ability, fear, supervision access, and venue type before generating any pool work.
training_implications.backend_use: Use these fields to select beginner safety records instead of fitness sets when competency is incomplete.

training_implications.implication: Beginner progression should unlock by demonstrated tasks, not by time spent or subjective motivation.
training_implications.backend_use: Require safe entry/exit, bubbles, front/back float recovery, glides, rolls, and short travel before continuous swim prescriptions.

training_implications.implication: For non-swimmers, the app should output supervised lesson prompts, safety education, confidence tasks, and instructor-referral guidance rather than solo workouts.
training_implications.backend_use: Create a non-swimmer template that never contains yardage, intensity, or deep-water assignments.

training_implications.implication: Breathing tasks should use brief, controlled repetitions with rest and support, not fatigue sets.
training_implications.backend_use: Use count-based bubbles, face wetting, and supported float recovery instead of timed underwater tasks.

training_implications.implication: Floating should appear in safety records and anxiety records, not only technique records.
training_implications.backend_use: Include cues for back floating, breathing control, signaling, and moving to safety when calm.

training_implications.implication: Fearful users need smaller steps, higher control, and optional repeats rather than automatic progression.
training_implications.backend_use: Use pre/post fear ratings and allow regression to prior tasks without marking failure.

training_implications.implication: Adult beginner instructions should avoid childlike framing and acknowledge previous negative experiences, privacy concerns, and goal differences.
training_implications.backend_use: Separate adult beginner language and recommended class types from child learn-to-swim copy.

training_implications.implication: For children, weak swimmers, and beginners, safety prompts should ask who is supervising, where they are positioned, and whether a lifeguard is present.
training_implications.backend_use: Do not show water tasks until supervision prerequisites are acknowledged.

training_implications.implication: Beginner plans should include pool rule knowledge and safe behavior checks alongside physical skills.
training_implications.backend_use: Add rule records for walking on deck, asking permission, obeying lifeguards, no pushing, no unsafe diving, and safe lane behavior.

training_implications.implication: Survival competence, water confidence, and stroke technique should be stored as separate progress tracks.
training_implications.backend_use: A user can be ready for survival sequences but not ready for freestyle volume; another can learn freestyle fragments while still needing safety gates.

training_implications.implication: Open-water sessions must require separate safety, venue, conditions, buddy, visibility, flotation, and exit checks.
training_implications.backend_use: Pool beginner completion should unlock pool fitness only, not open-water workouts.

training_implications.implication: After time away, injury, illness, growth, or fear return, users should repeat basic competency checks.
training_implications.backend_use: Create a return-to-water reassessment path before resuming prior swim plans.

training_implications.implication: Flotation aids, goggles, fins, or snorkels may help learning but cannot count as unsupported water competence.
training_implications.backend_use: Track aided and unaided completion separately.

training_implications.implication: Before swim recommendations, the app should screen for seizure disorder, cardiac concerns, medications affecting coordination, alcohol use, and other risk flags.
training_implications.backend_use: Risk flags should trigger supervision requirements, medical guidance copy, or no-solo-swim restrictions.

training_implications.implication: When the user is a non-swimmer or fearful beginner, qualified in-person lessons are the preferred path.
training_implications.backend_use: Recommend certified instruction, lifeguarded venue, appropriate class ratios, and observed skill feedback where available.
